label: Yirmeyahu (Jeremiah) — Part 3 — Chapters 16–23
summary_plain: YHWH tells Yirmeyahu: Do not take a wife or have children in this place — for those born here will die of deadly diseases. YHWH will hurl the people from this land into a land they have not known. But the days are coming when they will no longer say 'as YHWH lives who brought up the people from Mitsrayim' but 'as YHWH lives who brought up the people from the land of the north and from all lands.' Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of my pasture. I will raise up for Dawid a righteous Branch — he shall reign as king and deal wisely, and execute justice and righteousness in the land. His name: YHWH Tsidqenu — YHWH is our righteousness.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from the DSS Jeremiah manuscripts (4QJer-a through 4QJer-e) and the Orit Ge'ez. The false shepherds oracle (chapter 23) is a direct indictment of covenant leadership that scatters rather than gathers the people. The righteous Branch (Tsemah Tsaddiq) of 23:5 is the Davidic messianic expectation — a mortal king who executes justice. The Qumran community's messianic expectation, documented in 4Q174 (Florilegium) and 4Q252, describes this Branch as a human descendant of Dawid — not a divine figure. The second exodus prophecy (16:14-15) declares that YHWH's future ingathering will surpass the Mitsrayim exodus as the defining redemptive act.

key_terms.definition: YHWH sends Yirmeyahu to the potter's house; seeing the potter reshape a marred vessel, he receives the word: YHWH can reshape any nation including Yisra'el — the clay does not dictate its own form.
Yirmeyahu smashes a potter's jar at the Tofet gate before the elders as a sign: 'So will I break this people and this city, as one breaks a potter's vessel, so that it can never be mended.'
The priest Pashkhur, who oversees the Temple, beats Yirmeyahu and puts him in stocks after the smashed-jar prophecy; YHWH renames him 'Terror on Every Side' and declares he will die in Babylon.
Yirmeyahu's most extreme confession: he accuses YHWH of enticing him, says he is a laughingstock, then swings to trust, then curses the day he was born and the man who brought news of his birth.
Yirmeyahu 23:5-6 — YHWH will raise up for David a righteous Branch (Tsemakh Tzaddik) who will reign wisely and execute justice; his name will be 'YHWH Our Righteousness' (YHWH Tzidqenu).
The name of the coming Davidic leader in Yirmeyahu 23:6 — 'YHWH Our Righteousness'; a declaration that YHWH's own character of righteousness will be embodied in and enacted through this ruler.

Yirmeyahu 23 contains a sustained attack on false prophets: they speak visions from their own hearts, not YHWH's mouth; they say 'Peace' when YHWH has not sent them; they steal words from one another.
YHWH distinguishes in Yirmeyahu 23 between prophets who claim dreams as his word and the genuine prophet who has YHWH's word. 'What has straw in common with wheat, declares YHWH.'
Throughout Yirmeyahu 16-23, YHWH hints at a future restoration beyond the coming disaster; the full New Covenant promise comes in chapter 31, but the groundwork is laid here.

The Tofet in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom (south of Yerushalayim) where the people burned their children to Molokh; Yirmeyahu smashed the jar there; YHWH declares it will be called the Valley of Slaughter.

faq.question: What is the theological significance of the potter's workshop in Yirmeyahu 18?
faq.answer: The potter's workshop gives YHWH an answer to Yirmeyahu's theodicy questions: sovereignty. YHWH can reshape a nation as a potter reshapes clay. If YHWH announces disaster against a nation and that nation turns from evil, YHWH will relent; if he announces good and the nation does evil, he will reverse his announced good. The clay cannot dictate to the potter.

faq.question: Why did YHWH rename Pashkhur 'Terror on Every Side'?
faq.answer: After Pashkhur beat Yirmeyahu and put him in stocks, YHWH renamed him Magor-Missaviv (Terror on Every Side), declaring that he would see his friends fall by the sword and be carried to Babylon where he would die. The irony is sharp: Pashkhur silenced the prophet warning of terror; now his new name is terror itself.

faq.question: What is the Righteous Branch prophecy in Yirmeyahu 23?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 23:5-6 promises that YHWH will raise up a righteous Branch from David's line who will rule with wisdom and execute justice and righteousness. His name, 'YHWH Our Righteousness,' makes YHWH's own character the source and content of this ruler's reign. This is specifically a Davidic covenant promise within Yirmeyahu's condemnation of faithless kings.

faq.question: What is the difference between true and false prophecy according to Yirmeyahu 23?
faq.answer: In Yirmeyahu 23, false prophets speak from their own hearts ('visions of their own minds'), tell people there will be peace, have no standing in YHWH's council (the heavenly assembly), and steal words from one another. The true prophet has stood in YHWH's council and heard his actual word — which is like fire and like a hammer breaking rock, not smooth and comforting.

faq.question: Why is Yirmeyahu's extreme confession in chapter 20 preserved in the text?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 20:7-18 records a prophet accusing YHWH of deception, being overcome by YHWH's power, and cursing the day he was born. Its preservation is itself a statement about the Hebrew prophetic tradition: authentic covenant relationship with YHWH includes raw argument and complaint. Yirmeyahu does not suppress the darkness of prophetic suffering — he records it as part of the witness.

faq.question: What is the Valley of Ben-Hinnom and why was it condemned?
faq.answer: The Valley of Ben-Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom) south of Yerushalayim contained the Tofet, where people burned their children to Molokh. Yirmeyahu condemned it repeatedly (19:2-6; 7:30-34): YHWH declares he will rename it the Valley of Slaughter because so many will die there in the coming disaster. Its name was later contracted to Gehenna — an ancient Hebrew site of condemnation.

faq.question: What did YHWH mean by forbidding Yirmeyahu to mourn or enter a house of mourning?
faq.answer: In Yirmeyahu 16:5-7, YHWH forbids Yirmeyahu from entering houses of mourning or feasting — both normal social obligations. The sign's meaning: in the coming disaster, there will be so many dead that normal mourning will be impossible. Yirmeyahu's abstention from mourning is itself a prophetic act enacting the future where mourning rites will be overwhelmed.

faq.question: How does YHWH respond to Yirmeyahu's accusation of deception in chapter 20?
faq.answer: YHWH does not directly refute the accusation. After Yirmeyahu's extreme lament (20:7-13) YHWH swings through Yirmeyahu to a declaration of trust (20:11-13) before the final plunge into cursing his birth (20:14-18). The text preserves the oscillation without resolution — this is the authentic record of prophetic struggle, not a tidy theological statement.

faq.question: What is the pastoral significance of Yirmeyahu 23:24 — 'Do I not fill heaven and earth?'
faq.answer: YHWH's question — 'Can a man hide in secret places so I cannot see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth?' — confronts false prophets who prophesy in secret or claim YHWH said things he did not say. No hiding from YHWH is possible; his omnipresence is the foundation of prophetic accountability. It also grounds Yirmeyahu's confidence: the same YHWH who fills heaven and earth is with him.

faq.question: What does the Righteous Branch prophecy contribute to the messianic tradition?
faq.answer: Yirmeyahu 23:5-6 and the parallel in 33:15-16 contribute a specific emphasis to the Davidic tradition: the coming ruler's most defining characteristic is righteousness and justice, not military conquest. His name is YHWH's own righteousness. This locates the messianic hope firmly in YHWH's covenant character, not in human power — consistent with the Psalmic and Yesha'yahu strands of the tradition.

faq.question: Why does Yirmeyahu 20:20 say the man who brought news of his birth should be like the cities YHWH overthrew?
faq.answer: In 20:16, Yirmeyahu extends his curse to the man who told his father 'A son is born.' He wishes that man to become like the cities YHWH overthrew without pity. This is not literal but rhetorical — the full force of prophetic suffering. The life given to him has been a life of unrelenting opposition, ridicule, and suffering for delivering YHWH's word.
